 CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                     §

 MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,                §
 SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND
 WILLIAMSON COUNTIES


 CHRISTOPHER LANDGRAF, PRO SE (PARTY NO. 113) INITIAL POST-HEARING
                                         BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

      COMES NOW Christopher Landgraf, pro se, in the above-styled case, and

pursuant to SOAH Order No. 6, files this Initial Post-Hearing Brief and would like to

show the following:

                           INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

      I, Christopher Landgraf, submit this Initial Post-Hearing Brief in Docket No. 59475

against the proposed project overall but in support of Route 894, the ‘best meets’ route

selected by (“Applicants”) Oncor Electric Delivery Company, LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA




                                          Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                             PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                      SOAH Docket
                                                                                  No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                       Page 1 of 14
 Transmission Services Corporation (“LCRA”)1, in the event that the proposed project

was to move forward. I remain in strong opposition to any routes utilizing Links E3, E4,

and/or F41. Should Route 894 not be selected, I believe Route 487, the ‘best meets’

route selected by John Poole, P.E. (“PUC Staff”)2, is a reasonable alternative to Route

894.

                                            ARGUMENT

        Routes containing Links E3, E4, and/or F41 are poor choices

        Of the 122 Alternative Routes filed with the CCN application, Link E3 is contained

within 13 of the Alternative Routes, with E4 and F41 only appearing on Alternative

Routes that also include E33. After reviewing Applicant’s Notice of Errata4 (Link E3

containing Alternative Route 913 increasing in length from 1,271,079 to 1,271,140 feet),

the takeaway from Christopher Landgraf-Exhibit C remains the same; Alternative

Routes containing Link E3 are among the top 13 of 15 longest and costliest of the 122

Alternative Routes5. Additionally, of the 122 Alternative Routes, those that contained

Link E3 averaged 169 habitable structures within 500 feet of the route centerline versus

an average of 122 for routes not containing Link E36. It is my understanding that routes

that are longer, costlier, and with more habitable structures impacted (prudent

2 Commission Staff Exhibit 1-Direct Testimony of John Poole, P.E.
3 Joint Applicants Oncor & LCRA Exhibit 1
4 PUC Interchange Item No. 5342 – Applicants’ Notice of Errata
5 Christopher Landgraf Exhibit C

                                                                                   PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                            SOAH Docket
                                                                                        No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                             Page 2 of 14
 avoidance) are less desirable alternatives/poor choices (and that these are three of the

more important variables for consideration)7.

       Of the 29 RFI Routes, Link E3 is contained within two of the RFI Routes (Whitis

Routes 1-9 and 1-10), with E4 and F41 only appearing on RFI Routes that also include

E38. Of the 29 RFI Routes, Whitis Routes 1-9 and 1-10 are the top two longest and

most expensive9. While Whitis Routes 1-9 and 1-10 contain relatively low counts of 83

and 84 habitable structures within 500 feet of the route centerline, respectively, at costs

of $2,231,453,000 and $2,235,053,000, respectively, they are $373,685,000 and

$377,285,000, respectively, more expensive than Alternative Route Number 910 (the

most expensive of the 122 Alternative Routes at $1,857,768,000) 10. It’s hard to justify

the massive additional cost these routes have for their reduced habitable structure

counts. Additionally, Whitis Route 1-9 makes use of the problematic/controversial Link

J22 crossing of the Colorado River and Whitis Route 1-10 the Link J26 crossing 11; J22

and J26 are in the same vicinity of crossings that were rejected in Docket 37448 by the

Commission12.

       The Direct Testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke included link analysis of

protest forms, opposition letters, and intervenors13. Table RLSR – 24 in the Direct

Testimony shows that Link E3 was one of the top 20 Links identified by intervenors with

13 Cherokee Creek Partners Exhibit 1

                                                                                   PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                            SOAH Docket
                                                                                        No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                             Page 3 of 14
 E3 connecting upstream Links B3 and D2 also appearing and parallel Links C5 and E2

(alternative east/west Links to E3) not appearing in the list14. Table RLSR – 16 in the

Direct Testimony shows that Link E3 was one of the top 20 Links mentioned on Protest

Forms or Opposition Letters (2nd most), along with E3 connecting upstream Links B3

and D2 with the 3rd and 4th most, respectively15. This demonstrates strong opposition to

Link E3 and associated upstream connecting Links B3 and D2 compared to other link

options in the area.

        Christopher Landgraf – Exhibit D16 shows that Link E3 crosses 16 parcels and

only on 1 of the parcels (Parcel 2687) does the proposed centerline appear to run 100

foot off of an existing property line17. This results in only 814 feet for ‘length of link

parallel to apparent property boundaries’ on the ‘Links_Feet’ tab on the Applicant’s

spreadsheet18. Link E3 therefore performs poorly as link alternative from the

perspective of this metric.

        As stated in the Direct Testimony of Christopher Landgraf19, the applicants had

opportunity to update Link E3 following the Lampasas Public Participation Meeting to

coordinate with and/or more closely parallel Williamson County’s proposed Ronald

Reagan extension from IH-35 to SH-95 but failed to update Link E3 among many

others. Williamson County Exhibit A shows the Ronald Reagan extension as related to



14 Cherokee Creek Partners Exhibit 1, Page 81/Table RLSR - 24
15 Cherokee Creek Partners Exhibit 1, Page 83/Table RLSR - 16
16 Christopher Landgraf Exhibit D
17 Christopher Landgraf Exhibit D (from Direct Testimony Page 23)
18 Joint Applicants Oncor & LCRA Exhibit 23, ‘Links_Feet’ tab
19 Christopher Landgraf Exhibit G, Page 12/Line 19-Page 13/Line 14

                                                 Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                    PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                             SOAH Docket
                                                                                         No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                              Page 4 of 14
 Links in the area (partially showing Link E3)20. Coordinating and/or paralleling the

proposed roadway could have increased the attractiveness of Link E3 by paralleling the

proposed roadway, paralleling proposed apparent property boundaries, increased

parallel to compatible rights-of-way, and used the proposed roadway ROW to

buffer/increase distance from habitable structures (prudent avoidance). The inaction by

applicants on the topic kept Link E3 less attractive than it could have been compared to

other Alternative Links.

        Route 894 is the best route and Route 487 is a reasonable alternative

        Oncor/LCRA picked Route 894 as their ‘best meets’ route and they explain why

they chose it (no need for me to restate justifications they gave) 21. Route 487, the ‘best

meets’ route selected by PUC Staff22 (no need for me to restate justifications he gave),

is a reasonable alternative to Route 894. Neither of these routes makes use of Links

E3, E4, and/or F41 (which makes sense given how poorly routes containing E3 perform)

and both make use of Link C5 to travel east/west (parallel option/alternative to Link E3).

        Landowners proposing development in the area shouldn’t result in Link E3

route selection

        Whitis Land Investments, LP (Bruce Whitis)23, Hodge & Schwertner (James

Schwertner)24, and Solana Intervenors (Mary Alexander)25 state they have established


20 Williamson County Exhibit A
21 Joint Applicants Oncor & LCRA Exhibit 1
22 Commission Staff Exhibit 1-Direct Testimony of John Poole, P.E.
23 Whitis Land Investments, LP Exhibit 1, Page 7/Line 1 and Page 8/Lines 19-21
24 Hodge & Schwertner Exhibit 8, Page 4/Lines8-10
25 Solana Intervenors Exhibit 3, Page 10/Lines4-15

                                                Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                   PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                            SOAH Docket
                                                                                        No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                             Page 5 of 14
 MUDs and have development ambitions potentially impacted by Route 894 but none

have broken ground on the proposed developments and therefore it is my

understanding (from the hearing) that their proposed improvements should carry less

weight than existing conditions/other variables 26.

        Whitis Land Investments, LP (Bruce Whitis) states his “preferred route segments

follow D1, D2, E3, and F4” with “acceptable alternative segments (that) follow E2 to

F0”27. He also states that he opposes “use of Segments E13, E52, and F1 because the

segments do not take advantage of existing transmission line rights-of-way” 28 and

because his land is “well-suited to meet the growing need for affordable residential real

estate in the Salado area”29. Note that his acceptable alternative segments that follow

E2 to F0 would not make use of E3, E4, and/or F4130. While Links D1 (now split into

D11-D13) and D2 do parallel existing electric transmission lines, Links E3 and F4 (now

F41-45) do not31. Additionally, D1 and D2 route the powerline further south than

necessary, increasing parallel of existing transmission line rights-of-way with overall

route length and cost increase. Assuming the power line was routed down E13, E52

and/or F1, I would assume that the new homes built would be less expensive and

therefore result in housing that is more affordable than it would have been if the

powerlines weren’t located there (increasing affordable residential real estate).




26 BKV Cross Examination of Applicants’ Panel (6/8/2026, Page 27/Lines 16-22)
27 Whitis Land Investments, LP Exhibit 1, Page 3/Lines 16-18
28 Whitis Land Investments, LP Exhibit 1, Page 3/Lines 18-20
29 Whitis Land Investments, LP Exhibit 1, Page 3/Lines 22-23
30 Joint Applicants Oncor & LCRA Exhibit 22
31 Joint Applicants Oncor & LCRA Exhibit 23, ‘Links_Feet’ tab

                                                 Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                    PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                             SOAH Docket
                                                                                         No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                              Page 6 of 14
 Additionally, the installation of an air strip within a development of ‘affordable residential

real estate’ seems like an odd pairing to me and was questioned by Applicants, as

well32. Lastly, I wonder if the air strip was created simply to decrease the chances that

Links E13, E52, and/or F1 are chosen.

        Hodge & Schwertner (James Schwertner) state in their direct testimony that they

are against use of Link C5 and support use of Links B3, E3, and F41 instead 33. They

state that Link C5 would “create new internal divisions across multiple parcels rather

than following existing property boundaries or compatible rights-of-way” 34 and “impose

operational and fragmentation impacts”35 on their property. Comparing Link C5 to E3

using the ‘Links_Feet’ tab in the Applicant’s Excel table shows that the 41,610 foot long

Link C5 has 11,103 feet parallel to existing electric transmission lines, 3,043 feet

parallel to existing public roads/highways and 3,080 feet parallel to apparent property

boundaries while the 15,055 foot long Link E3 has 0 feet paralleled to existing electric

transmission lines, 0 feet parallel to existing public road/highways and only 814 feet

parallel to apparent property boundaries36; I would argue that this demonstrates that

Link E3 is more fragmenting than Link C5 and that C5 is a better link option compared

to Link E3. James Schwertner goes on to state “although Link C5 would affect our

property, if Links B3 and E3 are not selected, I would support its use as part of routes

such as the Applicants’ Route 894, which they identify as best addressing the PUC’s


32 Applicants’ Cross Examination of Bruce Whitis (6/11/2026, Page 60/Lines 6-10)
33 Hodge & Schwertner Exhibit 8, Page 12/Lines 22-26 and Page 14/Line 29
34 Hodge & Schwertner Exhibit 8, Page 13/Lines 4-5
35 Hodge & Schwertner Exhibit 8, Page 13/Lines 13-14
36 Joint Applicants Oncor & LCRA Exhibit 23, ‘Links_Feet’ tab

                                                 Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                    PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                             SOAH Docket
                                                                                         No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                              Page 7 of 14
 routing criteria”37 and he confirms that Link C5 is included in Route 894, the route Oncor

and LCRA TSC identified as the route that best addresses the PUC’s routing criteria 38.

Hodge & Schwertner (Brian C. Andrews) states in their direct testimony that they are

appearing in this proceeding on behalf of Schwertner Farms39 yet goes on to state that

“I recommend that the Commission approve Route 894 for the Bell County East Switch

to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project” 40; further reason for Link C5 to

be used instead of Links B3, E3, and F41.

        Solana Intervenors (Mary Alexander) state in their direct testimony that they

“explain how the proposed 765 kV transmission lines routes, especially including Route

894, would delay and impede the development and implementation of Solana Ranch” 41

and asks “the Commission to reject Route 894 or any route that traverses the interior of

the property”42 but does not state support for specific routes containing Link E3.

Additionally, Solana Intervenors (Joshua D. Rhodes, Ph.D.) state in their direct

testimony that they are testifying on behalf of Solana Ranch Company 43 and requests

that “the Commission reject Route 894 and instead order the construction of Route 392

as the more reasonable and balanced routing option”44. Applicants’ Excel table tab

‘Route Composition’ shows that Route 392 does not contain Link E3 45.

38 Hodge & Schwertner Exhibit 8, Page 12/Lines 18-21

         Additional commentary and recommendations

        As Link E3 performs poorly as an alternative routing option, I didn’t have to

spend my limited cross examination time to increase record for use to advocate against

its use as a routing option. I was instead able to somewhat (as much as a pro se

intervenor could do in limited 13, 7, and 3 minute durations) expand on the ideas that I

originally mentioned in my Direct Testimony, that a better value/more cost-effective

solution than the currently proposed project and related sister Permian Basin Reliability

Plan projects might exist46. Just as legislative action was taken in 1934 with the creation

of the overall LCRA organization, a new organization could be created, or LCRA scope

expanded, to operate additional natural gas pipelines and dispatchable natural gas fired

power plants to generate electricity in the Permian Basin/Import Path 2 areas, along

with local transmission projects, to possibly accomplish the Permian Reliability Plan

solution in a better value/most-effective way47. Additionally, I question if the need for

Import Path 2 still exists and if some of the initially forecasted electrical load is/will

actually be materializing48.

        As a Texas Registered Professional Engineer, it is my duty to protect the public

and Texas Administrative Code goes on to state the following:




46 Christopher Landgraf Exhibit G, Page 17/Line 6 to Page 18/Line 2
47 Christopher Landgraf Cross Examinations of Applicants’ Panel (6/8/2026, Pages 66-79), PUC Staff

(6/9/2026, Pages 260-266) and Barry T. Smitherman (6/11/2026, Pages 164-168)
48 Christopher Landgraf Cross Examinations of PUC Staff (6/9/2026, Pages 260-266) and Barry T.

Smitherman (6/11/2026, Pages 164-168)
                                               Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                  PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                           SOAH Docket
                                                                                       No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                            Page 9 of 14
        “(c) Engineers shall first notify involved parties of any engineering decisions or

       practices that might endanger the health, safety, property or welfare of the public.

       When, in an engineer’s judgment, any risk to the public remains unresolved, that

       engineer shall report any fraud, gross negligence, incompetence, misconduct,

       unethical or illegal conduct to the board or to proper civil or criminal authorities. 49”

During my cross examinations of the Applicant panel and PUC staff, I asked questions

related to induced AC50. PUC Staff’s recommendation that “Oncor and LCRA TSC shall

conduct surveys, if not already completed, to identify pipelines that could be affected by

the transmission lines and coordinate with pipeline owners in modeling and analyzing

potential hazards because of alternating-current interference affecting pipelines being

paralleled”51 does not go far enough to protect the public, in my opinion. The statement

should be expanded to say “Oncor and LCRA TSC shall conduct surveys, now and

routinely following the transmission line installation, to identify pipelines and similar

metallic objects that could be affected by the transmission lines and (1) coordinate with

pipeline/land owners in modeling and analyzing potential hazards because of

alternating-current interference affecting pipelines and similar metallic objects being

paralleled and (2) compensate pipeline/land owners for induced AC interference

mitigation”. It is my understanding that mitigation costs (capital during initial

transmission line construction and operation & maintenance following construction)




49 22 Texas Administrate Code § 137.55
50 Christopher Landgraf Cross Examinations of Applicants’ Panel and PUC Staff
51 Commission Staff Exhibit 1 – Direct Testimony of John Poole – Page 20/Lines 1-5

                                                Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                   PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                            SOAH Docket
                                                                                        No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                            Page 10 of 14
 could be recovered by the transmission line operators on future rate cases 52 so a

mechanism exists to compensate them for keeping the public safe.

       During his Cross Examination of Barry T. Smitherman53, Kevin Kennedy

questioned why habitable structures alone were used as a prudent avoidance metric

and why the number of occupants in the habitable structures weren’t instead used.

Discussing the example of a 1,000-bed hospital, Mr. Smitherman eventually stated that

if the “applicant, the commission, the judges are aware of that, that that would be on (sic

an) important consideration”. Additionally, during Kevin Kennedy’s Cross Examination

of Rae Lynn Reinecke54, Ms. Reinecke ended up not disputing that using the average

number of occupants for a given structure would be a better indicator for prudent

avoidance versus simply counting a structure. The PUC should consider updating how

prudent avoidance is assessed, moving from a simple habitable structure count to a

count of people, using readily/easily attainable data related to the density of people in

the habitable structures.

       Many questions were asked about notice and public meetings during the Cross

Examinations of Will McAdams55. While it appears the Applicants were compliant in that

they had at least one public meeting at the time the preliminary routes were available,

adding/changing links to impact new landowners and only giving those newly impacted

landowners notice at the time the Applicants formally submitted their application



52 Christopher Landgraf Cross Examination of PUC Staff
53 Kevin Kennedy Cross Examination of Barry T. Smitherman (6/11/2026, Pages 172-174)
54 Kevin Kennedy Cross Examination of Rae Lynn Reinecke (6/11/2026, Pages 230-234)
55 Cross Examinations of Will McAdams (6/11/2026, Pages 59-96)

                                               Initial Post-Hearing Brief of Christopher Landgraf, pro se
                                                                                  PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                                           SOAH Docket
                                                                                       No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                           Page 11 of 14
 (3/26/2026), in a process that had been legislatively reduced from the typical one year

to 180 day timeframe, it feels disingenuous to me when anyone says that all parties

were given a fair chance to participate in the process. The PUC should consider

increasing the area/boundary that Applicants are required to physically mail notice

about the public meeting(s) and not allow Link updates/adds that venture outside the

area of the initial physical mailings. This would allow all possibly impacted landowners

to participate in the public meeting(s) and possibly help shape the routes while also

giving all parties equal rights to legal representation (in this case, many parties were

unable to find legal representation because those typically doing CCNs amendments

were already conflicted out).

                                      CONCLUSION

       I remain against the proposed project overall but in support of Route 894, the

‘best meets’ route selected by Applicants, in the event that the proposed project was to

move forward. I remain in strong opposition of any routes utilizing Links E3, E4, and/or

F41. Should Route 894 not be selected, I believe Route 487, the ‘best meets’ route

selected by PUC Staff, is a reasonable alternative to Route 894. Additionally, I

respectfully request that the PUC update their statement regarding induced AC, on this

and future cases, that the PUC update their policy of use of habitable structures to

include average number of people per structure, when assessing prudent avoidance,

and that the PUC update their requirements on notice for public meetings/limit link

updates/adds to the area that initially received the notice.

         Additional commentary and recommendations


        As Link E3 performs poorly as an alternative routing option, I didn't have to

spend my limited cross examination time to increase record for use to advocate against

its use as a routing option. I was instead able to somewhat (as much as a pro se

intervenor could do in limited 13, 7, and 3 minute durations) expand on the ideas that I

originally mentioned in my Direct Testimony, that a better value/more cost-effective

solution than the currently proposed project and related sister Permian Basin Reliability

Plan projects might exist46. Just as legislative action was taken in 1934 with the creation

of the overall LCRA organization, a new organization could be created, or LCRA scope

expanded, to operate additional natural gas pipelines and dispatchable natural gas fired

power plants to generate electricity in the Permian Basin/Import Path 2 areas, along

with local transmission projects, to possibly accomplish the Permian Reliability Plan

solution in a better value/most-effective way47. Additionally, I question if the need for

Import Path 2 still exists and if some of the initially forecasted electrical load is/will

actually be materializing48.

                                      CONCLUSION

       I remain against the proposed project overall but in support of Route 894, the

'best meets' route selected by Applicants, in the event that the proposed project was to

move forward. I remain in strong opposition of any routes utilizing Links E3, E4, and/or

F41. Should Route 894 not be selected, I believe Route 487, the 'best meets' route

selected by PUC Staff, is a reasonable alternative to Route 894. Additionally, I

respectfully request that the PUC update their statement regarding induced AC, on this

and future cases, that the PUC update their policy of use of habitable structures to

include average number of people per structure, when assessing prudent avoidance,

and that the PUC update their requirements on notice for public meetings/limit link

updates/adds to the area that initially received the notice.
